But it doesn't stop there. Agents also introduce new challenges. They can give different answers to the same question, be confidently wrong without throwing an error, and turn one request into a long chain of model and tool calls that’s hard to debug. Every round trip costs more time and more tokens. Eventually the agent gives up.

The model isn’t the constraint. Context is.

Most security teams piece that answer together from scanner reports, spreadsheets, and a Slack thread asking who owns a service nobody recognizes, and you stay exposed for every hour that takes.

GitLab Orbit, now generally available, replaces this manual work with a single query. Orbit connects code, merge requests, pipelines, security findings, and ownership in one graph that stays current as your teams ship. Ask which projects are affected and who owns them, and you get an answer in minutes. Agents answer from the graph instead of crawling repositories and stitching together API calls, so they need fewer retries and fewer tokens to get there.

title: Prospero: a new coding harness for a more civilized age
summary: I’ve been fascinated with local LLMs for a couple of years now. The better open weight models, including some that inference on regular, higher-end consumer hardware at tolerable speeds, are now reliable enough to handle simpler programming tasks. This requires a coding harness, but so far this year I’ve been disappointed by all the harness offerings. For inexplicable reasons most are built with web stacks, and consume enormous amounts of memory. At its core a coding harness is essentially curl glued to popen(). This should not require gigabytes of RAM. So I built my own: Prospero. It’s written in my C++ style with a snappy Dear ImGui docking interface. It uses around two orders of magnitude fewer resources than other harnesses without sacrificing features.
